evidence.quote: Health Behaviors, Aging, & Cognition Lab The Hartman Research Group Our Focus The Health Behaviors, Aging, & Cognition Lab at UC San Diego studies how physical activity and sedentary behavior affect cognitive health, physical function, and biological aging — with a focus on cancer survivors and older adults. Our work spans large-scale clinical trials and the development of wearable-based interventions designed to fit into people’s everyday lives. Ongoing Research PACT: Physical Activity Counseling Tool PACT is developing a tool that turns patients’ Fitbit activity data into personalized, easy-to-use summaries for their healthcare providers. The goal is to make it simple for providers to review exercise trends and counsel patients on physical activity during routine visits. Patients’ activity data is connected with their electronic medical record, so providers have it on hand at every visit. This work is supported by the Allison and Robert Price Family and the Moores Cancer Center Clinical Trials Office Funding from Barbara Parker MD (MPIs Hartman & Larsen). I Can!: Improving Cognition through Activity I Can! was a 12-month randomized controlled trial testing whether a remotely delivered exercise program could improve cognitive functioning in 253 breast cancer survivors with self-reported cognitive difficulties. Participants were randomly assigned to either the exercise program or a health and wellness program. In addition to cognitive testing, the study also collected blood samples to examine whether exercise affects biological aging, building on earlier findings from Memory & Motion that linked physical activity to improved cognitive function in breast cancer survivors. The work is supported by the National Cancer Institute (R01CA225746, PI Hartman). We are currently conducting a long term follow-up study with the participants. Findings The exercise group increased their moderate-to-vigorous activity by about 35 minutes per week and showed greater improvements in objectively measured attention and memory, than the health & wellness group. A companion analysis found the exercise group also aged more slowly at the biological level. Using epigenetic clocks, which measure biological rather than chronological age, the exercise group showed about one month of biological aging over the 12-month study, compared to nearly 10 months in the health and wellness group.
